newsitem.title: USA: Local economies strong, labor tight - Fed banks.
newsitem.headline: Local economies strong, labor tight - Fed banks.

text.p: A close look at six of the nation's 12 economic districts suggests the economy appears to be headed for another year of firm economic growth in 1997, regional Federal Reserve bank officials said.
But in recent interviews, six regional Fed economists warned about continued tight local labour markets and scattered wage pressures.
The sentiment from local Fed officials provides some hints at which direction the nation's economy as a whole is moving, analysts said.

Scrutiny of the economy gained even more momentum among Wall Street pundits after the Fed hiked the federal funds rate -- which banks charge each other for overnight loans -- by one-quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent at the March 25 meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
Separate interviews were conducted with officials at the Federal Reserve Banks in Dallas, Richmond, Philadelphia, Kansas City, San Francisco and Minneapolis.
The six banks represent half of the nation's Federal Reserve System. They are responsible for covering the local economies of 32 of the nation's 50 states.

Some of the banks, however, are responsible for covering just specific parts of a given state. The Philadelphia Fed, for example, serves the entire state of Delaware, the eastern region of Pennsylvania and the southern portion of New Jersey.
Economists from four of the six banks -- San Francisco, Dallas, Kansas City and Richmond -- said they saw no real sign of a slowdown in local economies.

"We sense the economy in our district continues to operate at a healthy pace and we see no signs that we would see any substantial slowing in the region's growth," Kansas City Fed Vice President and economist Mark Drabenstott said.
Philadelphia and Minneapolis Fed economists said they expected somewhat slower growth in 1997 against 1996.

"The local economy has been growing fairly well for four years now ... (But) we see a few indications actually that the pace is a little slower than last year," said Edward Lotterman, regional economist at the Minneapolis Fed.

Labour markets also were seen tight pretty much across-the-board in all the regions surveyed. "I think the biggest cause for concern here would be the unusually tight labour markets," Richmond Fed economist Raymond Owens said.
There was one exception though at the 11th district, which is covered by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

Robert Valletta, an economist at the San Francisco Fed, said although labour markets were tight in the region, the unemployment level in California, the main state in the district, was still higher than the nation's average.

"The state is making up for the lost time ... but again it just has had so much further to go that in terms of the overall tightness of the labour market, we're still lagging behind much of the rest of the country," Valletta said.
Although labour markets remained tight, all regions surveyed downplayed the possibility of bottlenecks in the local economies.
Consumer spending in the regions surveyed appeared to be robust and, on average, was expected to remain strong in 1997.
"Consumers seem to be holding up fairly well," said Ted Crone, vice president and economist at the Philadelphia Fed.

"I think our biggest increase at least in sales in Pennsylvania and New Jersey actually was in the first half of last year. But it isn't that people have backtracked. They help up pretty well," Crone added.
D'Ann Petersen, economist at the Dallas Fed, said retail sales in her region was strong as well, suggesting investors were confident about the economy.
"Retail sales were not so good last year, but they're starting to pick up again," she said, adding that retailers have reported sales are growing at a "healthy rate."
All regions surveyed said, on average, that inflation continued to be moderate. None of the economists interviwed predicted a strong surge in price pressures.
"What we don't see broadly ... are rising prices across-the-board," Richmond Fed's Owens said.
"Certainly it's happening in some instances, but then we're seeing prices edging down in others.... But it doesn't appear that there is any unusual price pressure," he added.

Fed policy-makers will meet next on May 20 to decide on the course of interest rates. Although opinions are still mixed, many Wall Street experts believe the Fed will raise rates again at the May meeting by another quarter point in an effort to remain ahead of the inflation curve.
